summary.name: The infinite hows
summary.one_liner: An essay arguing against the Five Whys root-cause method in post-mortems and proposing "how?"-style questions and debriefing prompts as an alternative.
keywords: field guide to understanding human error
use_cases: Running a post-incident review without blaming individuals
Replacing Five Whys questions with open-ended how questions
Facilitating a debriefing after a production outage
Identifying critical junctures in an incident timeline
Learning human-factors concepts for software operations
summary.what_it_does: The essay critiques the Five Whys method, arguing that repeated "why?" questions lead to individual-blame answers and oversimplified linear causal chains. It recommends asking "how?" to collect people's own narratives, which it calls second stories, and to understand their local rationality. It proposes steps such as telling the story back to participants, identifying critical junctures, and probing what cues, knowledge, goals and expectations people had at each point. It includes debriefing prompt tables adapted from Sidney Dekker and Gary Klein, and cites Leveson, Hollnagel and Carroll on causes being constructed rather than found.
notable: Contrasts first stories (human error as cause) with second stories (human error as symptom of systemic vulnerabilities)
Provides a table of Gary Klein-style and Dekker-style debriefing facilitation questions
Links to four 45-minute tutorial videos given at Velocity New York
Epilogue draws on complexity theory and cites Dekker, Leveson and Carroll on root cause seduction
caveats: Essay is a critique and opinion piece, not a tool; no software or product is offered
Recommends the alternative approach but gives no formal step-by-step process beyond the outlined steps and prompts
Tutorials referenced are external and the page does not state their cost
